source.version: arXiv:2402.04975v1, 7 February 2024; CHI 2024 manuscript, full 20-page PDF. Cited supplementary appendices are not included and were not read.
source.title_on_document: ChatScratch: An AI-Augmented System Toward Autonomous Visual Programming Learning for Children Aged 6-12

supplement.where: Separate supplementary materials referenced on PDF p. 5 (Appendix A), p. 7 (Appendix B), and p. 12 (rubric details and Appendices D and E); no direct supplement URL is given.
supplement.holds: The paper directs readers to educator interview questions and thematic analysis in Appendix A, technical asset-quality evaluation procedures/results in Appendix B, Dr. Scratch scoring details, child video/interview thematic results in Appendix D, and data/analysis code in Appendix E. These materials are absent from this PDF, so additional statistics and allocation details could not be checked.

paper_design_summary: The main evaluation had 24 children create themed projects using both ChatScratch and original Scratch in a counterbalanced within-person design; the mechanism for assigning session orders is not stated (PDF p. 11, sections 5-5.2). Scratch educators rated the output assets, and the researchers counted visual elements and assessed code quality (PDF pp. 11-14, sections 5.3 and 6.1-6.2). The paper also reports a formative educator-interview study and summarizes a technical asset-set benchmark whose detailed methods/results are in an absent supplement (PDF pp. 4-5, section 3.1; p. 7, section 4.3).

studies.label: Main evaluation: counterbalanced within-child ChatScratch versus Scratch comparison

assignment.what_was_assigned: Each child used both ChatScratch and original Scratch in separate sessions. Tool and theme combinations were counterbalanced; the mechanism for assigning children to session orders is not stated. Counterbalancing is not treated as evidence of randomized order.
assignment.quote: Additionally, we incorporated a counterbalanced design, alternating between combinations of tools (ChatScratch or Scratch) and themes (A or B) to ensure unbiased results [69].
assignment.locator: PDF p. 11, sections 5 and 5.2 (Procedure); p. 12, section 5.4.1 (Data Analysis).

arms.name: ChatScratch
arms.description: AI-supported storyboard planning and visual cues, drawing with image polishing, and voice-based coding guidance with generated code templates. The same children also used Scratch (PDF p. 11, sections 5-5.2).

arms.name: Scratch
arms.description: Original Scratch platform with its built-in tutorials and assets. The same children also used ChatScratch (PDF p. 11, sections 5-5.2).

participants.who: Children aged 6-12, recruited via social media; all were native Mandarin speakers and Scratch beginners with less than 1 year of Scratch experience. Both condition counts refer to the same children.
participants.quote: We recruited 24 children (10 female, 14 male) as participants aged 6-12 years (M = 8.96, SD = 2.12).
participants.locator: PDF p. 11, sections 5 and 5.1: each child experienced both systems; p. 14, Figure 6: 24 scores per condition/aspect; p. 13, section 6.1: paired tests with 23 degrees of freedom.

ai_tool.name_model: ChatScratch: GPT4 and Stable Diffusion with ControlNet
ai_tool.how_used: Multiple forms of assistance: generated visual cues for story planning, image generation to polish children's doodles while retaining their outlines and positions, and a Scratch-specialized GPT4 assistant giving spoken coding guidance and editable Scratch code templates. PDF pp. 7-9, sections 4.2-4.5.

task.description: Create personally meaningful Scratch story projects on Memorable Experiences and Animal Stories, including planning, creation of visual assets (sprites and backdrops), and programming. The creative output ratings concern the assets. PDF p. 11, sections 5.2 and 5.3.2.
task.duration: Two sessions separated by 48 hours; approximately 70 minutes per session, including a 30-minute autonomous creative programming task (PDF p. 11, section 5.2).

contrasts.reported: ChatScratch mean 3.96 (SD 0.55) versus Scratch mean 2.67 (SD 1.01); paired t(23) = 6.33. Table 3 prints p = 0.000** with a Bonferroni-correction note; section 6.1 reports p < 0.01. Three Scratch educators assessed assets on a 5-point Likert scale.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 14, Table 3 (Creativity row and notes) and Figure 6; p. 13, section 6.1; p. 11, section 5.3.2 (raters, scale and definition).

outcomes.name: Expert-rated asset originality (own creation rather than sourced resources)
outcomes.question: with_ai

contrasts.reported: ChatScratch mean 4.29 (SD 0.86) versus Scratch mean 2.17 (SD 0.87); paired t(23) = 13.06. Table 3 prints p = 0.000** with a Bonferroni-correction note; section 6.1 reports p < 0.01. Originality is defined as the extent to which assets reflect the child's own creation rather than existing resources.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 14, Table 3 (Originality row and notes) and Figure 6; p. 13, section 6.1; p. 11, section 5.3.2 (definition).

outcomes.name: Project richness: visual element count (sprites plus backdrops)
outcomes.question: with_ai

contrasts.reported: ChatScratch mean 4.81 (SD 2.34) versus Scratch mean 3.06 (SD 1.34); paired t(23) = 5.40, p < 0.01. The count is the sum of sprites and backdrops within a child's project.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 13, section 6.1, first paragraph; p. 11, section 5.3.1 (measure definition).

outcomes.name: Expert-rated asset consistency (alignment with project-planning descriptions)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Following Amabile's Consensual Creativity Assessment Technique, three Scratch educators independently rated the assets on a 5-point Likert scale. Consistency measures the extent to which the assets align with the child's descriptions during project planning (PDF p. 11, section 5.3.2).

contrasts.reported: ChatScratch mean 4.04 (SD 0.62) versus Scratch mean 2.79 (SD 1.38); paired t(23) = 4.22. Table 3 prints p = 0.001** with a Bonferroni-correction note; section 6.1 reports p < 0.01. The same 24 children completed both conditions; Figure 6 reports 24 scores per condition/aspect.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 11, sections 5-5.2 (same children, assistance and session timing) and 5.3.2 (definition, raters and scale); p. 13, section 6.1; p. 14, Table 3 (Consistency row and notes) and Figure 6.

outcomes.name: Expert-rated asset quality
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Following Amabile's Consensual Creativity Assessment Technique, three Scratch educators independently rated the assets on a 5-point Likert scale. Quality covers the inherent attributes of the assets, including completeness, clarity, detail and harmony (PDF p. 11, section 5.3.2).

contrasts.reported: ChatScratch mean 4.13 (SD 0.74) versus Scratch mean 4.08 (SD 0.72); paired t = 0.20, p = 1, as printed in Table 3 with a Bonferroni-correction note. The same 24 children completed both conditions; Figure 6 reports 24 scores per condition/aspect.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 11, sections 5-5.2 (same children, assistance and session timing) and 5.3.2 (definition, raters and scale); p. 13, section 6.1 (means and SDs); p. 14, Table 3 (Quality row and notes) and Figure 6.

studies.label: Formative investigation: Scratch educator interviews and classroom observations

assignment.what_was_assigned: No AI-assistance conditions: recruited educators were interviewed after classroom observations to identify design requirements.
assignment.quote: We recruited six expert Scratch educators (3 females, 3 males) of age 26-39 (M=31, SD=4.44) with Scratch teaching experience range from 4 to 12 years (M=6.67, SD=2.96).
assignment.locator: PDF pp. 4-5, section 3.1 (Method): educator recruitment, classroom observations and interviews.

arms.name: Educator interviews
arms.description: Single formative interview sample; no AI intervention or comparison conditions.

participants.who: Experienced Scratch educators affiliated with a tutoring company in China specializing in programming for children; classroom observations informed their interviews. The number of children observed is not reported.
participants.quote: We recruited six expert Scratch educators (3 females, 3 males) of age 26-39 (M=31, SD=4.44) with Scratch teaching experience range from 4 to 12 years (M=6.67, SD=2.96).
participants.locator: PDF p. 4, section 3.1 (sample); p. 5, section 3.1 (interview transcripts analyzed thematically).

ai_tool.name_model: No AI assistance assigned to participants
ai_tool.how_used: Whisper and GPT-4 were used by researchers for transcription and translation of interviews, not as a creative-task intervention (PDF p. 5, section 3.1).

task.description: Classroom observations and educator interviews about barriers to children's autonomous Scratch learning, analyzed thematically for design implications; no scored creativity or diversity outcome (PDF pp. 4-6, section 3).
task.duration: Educator interviews lasted 41-54 minutes (PDF p. 5, section 3.1).

studies.label: Technical asset-quality benchmark (summary only; supplementary methods absent)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Asset sets were compared; no assignment of people to AI assistance is described. The main text does not establish whether the ChatScratch benchmark assets came from a separate model-only generation exercise or the child study.
assignment.quote: We collected materials from both the built-in library and the Scratch community, and calculated the FID and SWD scores between them as references.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 7, section 4.3, final paragraph; detailed procedures deferred to supplementary Appendix B, absent from this PDF.

arms.name: ChatScratch-generated assets
arms.description: Generated assets compared with the Scratch built-in reference set; asset and human sample counts not reported in the main text.

arms.name: Scratch community assets
arms.description: Collected community assets compared with the same built-in reference set; AI-use status of their creators is not stated.

arms.name: Scratch built-in library assets
arms.description: Reference asset collection used for both image-set comparisons; no participant condition.

participants.who: Asset collections, not an enumerated human sample. Neither people counts nor asset counts are reported for this benchmark in the main text.
participants.quote: We collected materials from both the built-in library and the Scratch community, and calculated the FID and SWD scores between them as references.

ai_tool.name_model: ChatScratch image generation: Stable Diffusion with ControlNet
ai_tool.how_used: The system generates polished assets from descriptions and doodles; the precise benchmark sampling and generation procedure is deferred to supplementary Appendix B (PDF p. 7, section 4.3).

task.description: Technical comparison of asset quality using Frechet Inception Distance (FID) and Sliced Wasserstein Distance (SWD), with built-in Scratch assets as the reference. The main text states that ChatScratch-generated assets had superior results to community assets but provides no numerical statistics; those procedures/results are in supplementary Appendix B (PDF p. 7, section 4.3).

company_involvement.description: The formative educators were affiliated with a tutoring company in China specializing in programming for children. The acknowledgments credit Gang Dai, Wen Meng and Xuenan Jiang from AC Source Programming for expert educational perspectives and assistance with the experiment. These passages document educational and experimental assistance; funding from the company is not stated.
company_involvement.locator: PDF p. 4, section 3.1 (educators affiliated with a tutoring company in China); p. 18, Acknowledgments (AC Source Programming assistance).

eligibility.reason: The main comparison analyzed 24 unique children, below the required 50; the same children completed both conditions, so the arm counts must not be added (PDF p. 11, sections 5-5.2; p. 14, Figure 6; p. 13, section 6.1). The methods describe counterbalancing and alternating tool/theme combinations but do not state random assignment to session orders or an explicit mechanism for allocating children to those orders, leaving criterion 1 unclear (PDF p. 11, section 5.2; p. 12, section 5.4.1). Criterion 3 is met because Scratch educators scored creativity and originality on the produced assets (PDF p. 11, section 5.3.2; p. 14, Table 3). The formative interviews do not test AI assistance, and the technical benchmark supplies neither a human sample size nor sufficiently detailed methods to classify a separate contextual comparison (PDF pp. 4-5, section 3.1; p. 7, section 4.3).

one_line_finding: Among 24 children using both systems, ChatScratch assets received higher expert creativity scores than Scratch assets, 3.96 (SD 0.55) versus 2.67 (SD 1.01), paired t(23) = 6.33, p < 0.01; random assignment to session orders is not stated (PDF p. 11, sections 5.1-5.2; p. 13, section 6.1; p. 14, Table 3).
